abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a foundational paradigm shift in modeling trustworthiness for autonomous systems by introducing the Probabilistic Temporal Trust Calculus (PTTC), a novel theoretical framework that transcends traditional static trust assessment methods. Unlike existing approaches that evaluate system reliability at discrete time intervals, PTTC captures the continuous evolution of trust dynamics in safety-critical environments through temporal probabilistic logic. The framework integrates formal verification principles with stochastic process theory to model how trust propagates across interdependent components in cyber-physical systems operating under adversarial conditions. We formalize the semantics of trust transitions using μ-calculus extensions, enabling rigorous reasoning about system behavior over infinite execution traces. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that PTTC provides sound and complete characterization of trust degradation patterns in complex AI-enabled systems, addressing fundamental limitations in current dependable computing models. The framework's applicability extends to hardware security verification where it can reason about side-channel leakage evolution. We prove critical properties including trust monotonicity conditions and convergence guarantees that establish necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving acceptable confidence levels. This paradigm establishes a new theoretical foundation for designing verification and validation procedures that account for dynamic trust evolution, fundamentally changing how we approach confidence assessment in autonomous operations.

This paper presents a significantly enhanced theoretical framework for reliability analysis of fault-tolerant systems operating in hostile environments, addressing critical limitations in conventional reliability block diagrams when applied to modern cyber-physical systems with intricate failure dependencies. While existing reliability models assume independent failure modes, real-world safety-critical systems exhibit complex dependent failures arising from shared hardware resources, software vulnerabilities, and environmental stressors. We propose the Enhanced Dependent Failure Reliability Model (EDFRM) that integrates Bayesian networks with traditional reliability theory to capture these intricate failure correlations. The theoretical framework incorporates common cause failure analysis, cascading fault propagation, and recovery mechanism dependencies into a unified probabilistic framework. Our analysis derives closed-form expressions for system reliability under various dependency structures, substantially improving upon Monte Carlo simulation approaches that dominate current practice. The model provides significantly tighter bounds on reliability estimates for redundant architectures in autonomous vehicles and industrial control systems. We demonstrate through extensive theoretical analysis that EDFRM reduces estimation error by up to 47% compared to independence-assuming models while maintaining computational tractability for large-scale systems. The framework's integration with formal verification enables rigorous safety argumentation for certification of safety-critical systems.

This paper introduces SecureCPS, a groundbreaking architectural framework for cyber-physical systems that fundamentally reconceptualizes security enforcement through a novel separation between functional correctness and security verification at the hardware-software boundary. Current approaches to securing cyber-physical systems rely predominantly on software-based security measures that operate independently of the formal verification pipeline, creating systematic gaps between verified properties and runtime security enforcement. SecureCPS introduces a hardware security co-processor that implements formally verified security monitors directly in the trusted computing base, establishing an immutable security enforcement layer that operates concurrently with functional system execution. The architecture employs a domain-specific language for specifying security-critical properties that are automatically compiled into runtime monitors verified through theorem proving. Unlike existing secure computing architectures that treat security as an add-on feature, SecureCPS fundamentally integrates security enforcement into the system design verification flow, ensuring that formal verification evidence directly translates to runtime guarantees. We present a complete reference implementation on RISC-V architecture demonstrating the framework's applicability to safety-critical embedded systems. Security analysis confirms the architecture provides provable protection against control-flow hijacking and data exfiltration attacks while maintaining the real-time performance requirements of industrial control systems.

This paper presents ResilientEdge, an improved edge computing framework for resilient operation of autonomous systems in contested network environments, substantially advancing the state-of-the-art in fault-tolerant distributed computing for safety-critical applications. Existing edge computing architectures for autonomous systems suffer from significant vulnerabilities during network degradation, including complete service unavailability and cascading failures when communication links fail. ResilientEdge introduces a hierarchical redundancy architecture with three novel mechanisms: adaptive task migration based on real-time confidence estimation, Byzantine-fault-tolerant consensus for state synchronization, and predictive resource provisioning using learned failure models. The improved design significantly enhances upon prior work by integrating software security mechanisms directly into the fault tolerance framework, addressing an important gap where existing resilient systems treat security and reliability as orthogonal concerns. We implement ResilientEdge on a heterogeneous computing platform combining ARM processors with FPGA acceleration, demonstrating substantial improvements in system availability from 94.2% to 99.7% under adversarial network conditions while reducing worst-case recovery latency by 62%. The framework's verification and validation methodology combines formal model checking for protocol correctness with extensive simulation-based testing across diverse failure scenarios. Performance evaluation on autonomous vehicle platooning applications confirms the system's ability to maintain safe operational boundaries even under sustained cyber attacks targeting communication infrastructure.
